meta.title: Running the orders database
meta.description: The runbook for our production PostgreSQL cluster: how backups and restores work, how failover happens and how we upgrade without losing data.
meta.author: Meridian Freight, Data platform team

summary: The orders database is a three-node PostgreSQL 16 cluster managed by Patroni, with continuous WAL archiving so we can restore to any second in the last 14 days. A failed primary is replaced automatically in about 30 seconds. Minor upgrades are a rolling restart; major upgrades use logical replication to a new cluster so the switch takes minutes, not hours.

meta.question: How are the orders database backups taken, and how do we restore one?
meta.title: Backups and restores

answer.headline: pgBackRest takes a full backup every Sunday and a differential every night, and archives WAL continuously, so we can restore to any point in the last 14 days and lose at most 60 seconds of writes.
answer.text: A backup only counts once it has been restored. A scheduled job restores last night's backup to a scratch server every Monday and checks the row counts against production.
points: Recovery point objective: 60 seconds; recovery time objective: 2 hours
Backups are encrypted and copied to a second region
Replicas are not backups: a bad `DELETE` reaches them in milliseconds

blocks.title: Check the archive, not just the backup
blocks.label: Watch
blocks.body: If WAL archiving fails, backups still succeed but point-in-time recovery has a gap, and `pg_wal` fills the disk. The `pg_stat_archiver` alert pages when `failed_count` rises or the last archived segment is older than 5 minutes.

blocks.title: Restoring to a point in time

items.title: Agree the target time
items.text: Find the last good moment from the application logs, for example just before a bad migration ran. Write it in the incident channel.

items.title: Restore to a new server
items.text: Never restore over production. Provision a scratch server from the `pg-restore` template.

items.title: Check the data
items.text: Start PostgreSQL, let recovery finish and compare the affected tables with what the team expects.

items.title: Copy back or promote
items.text: For a few rows, copy them back with `COPY`. For the whole database, promote the restored server and repoint the application.

blocks.title: Weekly restore test duration
blocks.caption: Time to restore last night's backup to a scratch server. The objective is under 2 hours.

blocks.title: Restore time is creeping up
blocks.label: Trend
blocks.body: The database grows by about 40 GB a month, and restore time follows it. At this rate we reach the 2-hour objective in spring 2027; the plan is to take full backups twice a week from January.

meta.question: What happens when the primary database fails?
meta.title: Failover

answer.headline: Patroni notices the primary has stopped renewing its leader lock and promotes the most up-to-date replica within about 30 seconds; the application reconnects through the load balancer without a config change.
answer.text: The cluster has one primary and two streaming replicas in different availability zones. Patroni stores the leader lock in etcd, so only one node can ever be primary.
points: One replica is synchronous, so a committed order is never lost on failover
Writes fail for about 30 seconds; the application retries them
You almost never need to act; check that the old primary rejoins as a replica

blocks.title: The cluster
blocks.caption: Step through a failover: pg-1 stops renewing its lock and pg-2, the synchronous replica, takes over.

meta.title: Orders database cluster
meta.description: The application connects through HAProxy, which asks Patroni which node is primary. Patroni keeps the leader lock in etcd.

steps.title: Normal running
steps.description: Writes go to pg-1, which streams WAL to both replicas.

steps.title: Promotion
steps.description: pg-1 stops renewing its lock. After the 30-second TTL, pg-2, the synchronous replica, takes the lock and is promoted.

steps.title: Traffic moves
steps.description: HAProxy's health check now sees pg-2 as primary and sends writes there.

items.text: Run `patronictl list` and confirm one Leader and two replicas streaming
Check the old primary rejoined; if not, `patronictl reinit orders pg-1`
Confirm replication lag is under 1 MB on both replicas
Find out why the primary failed before closing the incident

blocks.title: Never promote by hand while Patroni is running
blocks.label: Danger
blocks.body: Running `pg_ctl promote` yourself can leave two primaries accepting writes, and their data then has to be merged by hand. Use `patronictl switchover` or `patronictl failover`, which take the lock first.

meta.question: How do we upgrade PostgreSQL without a long outage?
meta.title: Upgrades

answer.headline: Minor versions are a rolling restart, replicas first, with one 30-second switchover. Major versions are copied to a new cluster with logical replication and switched over in a planned window of about 5 minutes.
answer.text: Minor releases (16.4 to 16.5) only fix bugs and security issues, and share the on-disk format, so they are safe to apply quickly. Major releases (16 to 17) change the format and need either `pg_upgrade` or a copy.
points: Apply minor releases within 30 days of release
Plan a major upgrade every year; each major version is supported for 5 years
Every major upgrade is rehearsed on a restored copy first

options.name: pg_upgrade --link
options.summary: Upgrade the data files in place.
cons: The database is down for the whole upgrade

options.name: Logical replication
options.summary: Build a new cluster on the new version and stream changes into it.
pros: Old cluster stays as a fallback
Can test the new version with real data
cons: Sequences and schema changes need care
Twice the servers for a week
options.verdict: Our standard for the orders database

items.title: Build the new cluster
items.text: Three new nodes on the new version, schema copied with `pg_dump --schema-only`.

items.title: Start replication
items.text: Create a publication on the old primary and a subscription on the new one. The initial copy takes about 6 hours.

items.title: Freeze schema changes
items.text: No migrations until the switch; logical replication does not copy DDL.

items.title: Switch over
items.text: Stop writes, wait for zero lag, copy sequence values, point HAProxy at the new cluster.

items.title: Keep the old cluster for 7 days
items.text: Then remove it once nothing has needed it.
